content_metadata.description: This animated video narrates the process of the Citric Acid Cycle, using cartoon characters to represent various molecules involved in cellular respiration.

qAndA.question: What color are the molecules of pyruvate?
How many Pyruvate molecules enter the Citric Acid Cycle?
How many carbon molecules does Oxaloacetate have?
Which molecule acts as an escort for Pyruvate to enter the Mitochondria?
What is the final molecule left in the cycle, which allows for it to repeat?

scenes.contextualRelevance: Introduction to the Citric Acid Cycle and setting the stage for the animation.

narrativeProgression.description: NADH introduces the Citric Acid Cycle as the second part of a Cellular Respiration play.
NADH describes that in the Citric Acid Cycle, 2 Pyruvate molecules enter the Mitochondria, which is represented in the animation by the area inside the wooden fence.
NADH mentions that the Pyruvate molecules need an escort to enter the Mitochondria and points out the Purple Monster as the one responsible.

NADH explains that the play will demonstrate what happens to the Pyruvate molecules, from entering the Citric Acid Cycle with Coenzyme A, to the transformation of Oxaloacetate to Citrate, and back to Oxaloacetate.
NADH jokingly mentions their lack of acting skills and their true calling in conducting experiments to "rule the world."
NADH encourages the audience to enjoy the second part of the play, the Citric Acid Cycle, and to stay tuned for the summary.

scenes.title: Introduction and Setup

activities.description: Pyruvate move towards the mitochondria fence
Coenzyme A removes a carbon from each Pyruvate molecule
Acetyl CoA links up to Oxaloacetate to form Citrate

characterInteraction.description: Coenzyme A acts as an escort for the Pyruvate molecules, taking them inside the mitochondria and removing a carbon from each Pyruvate molecule.
Acetyl CoA enters the mitochondria and links up to Oxaloacetate to form Citrate.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Detailed representation of how molecules are transformed and transported within the Citric Acid Cycle.

narrativeProgression.description: The two pyruvate molecules move toward the mitochondria fence in order to enter the citric acid cycle, but they need to be escorted into the cycle. Coenzyme A is a molecule that acts as an escort for these molecules.
When CoA attaches to the pyruvate, it removes a carbon that’s lost to CO2 waste. The resulting two carbon molecules linked to CoA are called acetyl CoA.

Acetyl CoA enters the citric acid cycle where the CoA lets go and the two carbon molecules link up to a four carbon molecule called oxaloacetate to form a six carbon molecule called citrate or citric acid.

scenes.thematicElements: Transportation and Transformation of molecules in the Citric Acid Cycle.
scenes.title: Molecule Transformation - Part 1

activities.description: NAD+ pick up an electron from Citrate and become NADH
NADH heads to the electron transport chain
Citrate lose a carbon to CO2 waste and become a 5 carbon molecule
Citrate lose a carbon to CO2 waste and become a 4 carbon molecule
A phosphate group is added to ADP becoming ATP
FAD pick up an electron from Citrate and become FADH2
FADH2 heads to the electron transport chain
NAD+ pick up an electron from Citrate and become NADH
NADH heads to the electron transport chain

characterInteraction.description: NAD+ molecules interact with Citrate, picking up an electron from the molecules, transforming them into NADH, and triggering their departure towards the electron transport chain.
FAD molecule interact with Citrate, picking up an electron from the molecules, transforming into FADH2, and triggering its departure towards the electron transport chain.
ADP receives a phosphate group from Citrate, resulting in its transformation into ATP.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Showcasing the processes of electron transfer, energy production, and the cyclic nature of the Citric Acid Cycle.

narrativeProgression.description: NAD+ picks up an electron from citrate and becomes NADH, heading to the electron transport chain.
Citrate loses a carbon molecule to CO2 and becomes a five-carbon molecule. It loses another carbon molecule to CO2 and becomes a four-carbon molecule.
A phosphate group is added to an ADP molecule, making ATP.
FAD picks up an electron to become FADH2 and heads to the electron transport chain.
NAD+ picks up an electron, becomes NADH, and heads to the electron transport chain.
The four-carbon molecule left in the cycle is oxaloacetate, which can link to another acetyl molecule, and the cycle repeats.

scenes.thematicElements: Electron Transfer, Energy Production, Cyclic Process in the Citric Acid Cycle.
scenes.title: Molecule Transformation - Part 2

scenes.contextualRelevance: Recap of the Citric Acid Cycle and setting up the narrative for subsequent processes in cellular respiration.

narrativeProgression.description: NADH, the narrator, summarizes the Citric Acid Cycle, highlighting the use of 2 Pyruvate molecules, the creation of 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 6 CO2.
NADH emphasizes that NADH and FADH2 will proceed to the Electron Transport Chain for further energy production.
NADH explains the transformation of Oxaloacetate combined with Acetyl, forming Citrate, which then undergoes changes, culminating in its return to Oxaloacetate, thus completing the cycle.
NADH mentions the production of ATP, NADH, FADH2, and CO2 during this cyclic process.
NADH concludes the summary, mentioning other experiments to attend to and anticipating a "final performance" in part 3, focusing on the Electron Transport Chain.

scenes.thematicElements: Summary of key molecules and processes involved in the Citric Acid Cycle and a transition to the Electron Transport Chain.
scenes.title: Summary and Conclusion

climax.description: A phosphate group is added to an ADP molecule, making ATP.
